sections.html:
• Excellent clean-up crew: eats algae and leftover fish food.
  • Beginner-friendly and tolerant of a wide range of water parameters.
  • Very easy to breed.
  • Small enough for a nano tank of about 8 litres.

Many colour morphs are now available, such as red, orange, yellow, green jade, blue dream, blue velvet, chocolate, black rose and rili (striped). Red is the most popular colour, which is why the species is commonly known as "cherry shrimp" or "red cherry shrimp" (RCS). Colour grades such as sakura red, fire red, painted fire red and Bloody Mary are very subjective. The best way to judge colour is to see the shrimp in person and pick those that look best to you.

Do not pick only the biggest, most colourful shrimp, because they might all be females or might be too old to breed for much longer.
Neocaridina davidi is native to China and Taiwan. The wild form normally has a translucent body covered in mottled brown speckling that blends in well with its surroundings.

Neocaridina shrimp can fit in tiny tanks, but a tank of about 40 litres or larger is preferred for a healthy breeding colony. Ideally use a mature tank that has been running for many months, full of microfauna and mulm to graze on.

After molting, the new exoskeleton is soft, so the shrimp hide until the new shell hardens. Provide lots of live plants, shrimp caves and other shelter. Dense plants such as mosses also grow algae and biofilm, which cherry shrimp love to forage on.

A shrimp molt is clear and translucent with a split in the middle of the back, whereas a dead shrimp is fully opaque. Many hobbyists leave the old exoskeleton in the tank because the shrimp eat it to gain extra calcium for their next molt.

Shrimp have a hard outer exoskeleton and must molt regularly when they outgrow their old "skin". To build the new exoskeleton they prefer pH 6.5–8.5, GH of at least 6 dGH and KH of at least 2 dKH. In soft water, add mineral supplements to prevent failed molts (sometimes called the "white ring of death", when a dead shrimp has a white band or gap behind its head). Crushed coral helps raise KH, while Wonder Shell and Seachem Equilibrium raise GH.

Neocaridina davidi can easily live at 16–28°C, so in most cases an unheated aquarium is fine. They are most comfortable at 22–24°C. Temperature greatly affects metabolism: at higher temperatures they grow faster but live shorter lives, and at lower temperatures they live longer but breed less.

Use a sponge filter, or cover the filter intake with a pre-filter sponge so that no baby shrimp are accidentally sucked up. A heater is only needed if the room temperature is below 22–24°C and you want to maximise reproduction.

As detritivores, they constantly scavenge for algae, decaying animal and plant matter, biofilm and other edible organics. They readily eat any community fish food dropped in the tank, but also feed shrimp-specific foods such as Hikari Shrimp Cuisine and Xtreme Shrimpee Sinking Sticks, which are enriched with calcium and other minerals to aid molting. Repashy gel food and vegetables such as blanched zucchini are good for long-term grazing because they stay stable in water for longer.

Include enough protein in the diet, because juveniles need it for growth and females use it to make eggs. Baby shrimp, especially newborns, do not move much and can easily be outcompeted for food, so give them a variety of powdered foods, such as Hikari First Bites, Easy Fry and Small Fish Food, and Bacter AE, that drift toward them. Botanicals such as catappa leaves and cholla wood break down quickly and grow a layer of biofilm that is an excellent food source for both young and adult shrimp.

If you plan to start a breeding colony, get at least 10 shrimp, which should ensure both males and females.

Almost all fish will eat baby shrimp, so for optimal breeding keep them in a species-only tank. If you mainly want to keep adult shrimp and do not mind how many young are produced, certain peaceful, small species can work as tank mates, such as other dwarf shrimp, snails, otocinclus catfish, chili rasboras and other nano fish. Cherry shrimp have also been kept in a community tank with guppies and neon tetras.

Females are larger, grow up to 4 cm and display very bright, vivid colours. In adulthood the female either has a yellow, saddle-like shape on her back (unfertilised eggs in the ovaries) or is "berried" and carries fertilised eggs on the swimmerets under her tail. Males are smaller at 2.5–3 cm, have a slimmer tail and are more translucent. Juveniles are hard to sex since they all look slender and less colourful than adults.

Dwarf shrimp reproduce very easily: females carry about 20–30 eggs at a time and the adults do not prey on their own young. Keep both sexes, feed plenty of good food and remove any predators that may eat the babies.

When a female has molted and is ready to spawn, she releases pheromones, and the adult males swim around in a frenzy looking for her. After mating she becomes berried and carries the eggs under her tail for about a month, depending on temperature. She fans fresh water over the eggs with her swimming legs to clean them and prevent fungal or bacterial growth. The babies hatch as exact replicas of the adults, but less colourful and only 2 mm long. Feed them powdered foods and catappa leaves, and they soon grow big enough to eat regular shrimp foods.

If breeding stops, the colony may have reached its maximum capacity for the amount of food provided. Either feed more (and perhaps upgrade the tank) or move some shrimp out.

To get redder shrimp, once the population is a healthy size, cull the less colourful ones so only the brightest red (or other colour) shrimp pass on their traits. Without culling, populations often degrade in appearance over time.
